extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent applicants, USPTO examiners, policymakers, and litigators concerned with U.S. §101 subject-matter eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and proposed legislative reform of 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility under the Mayo/Alice framework, with guidance on how courts and the USPTO should analyze inventive concepts, claim dissection, and the role of §§102/103/112. Aimed at clarifying eligibility rules across technologies (software, life sciences, mechanical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept—such as a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea. Step 2: If so, determine whether there is an 'inventive concept … sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the ineligible concept itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the controlling Supreme Court test applied by lower courts; courts analyze whether claim subject matter falls within judicial exceptions, then ask whether additional claim elements supply an inventive concept. Examples in the text show courts applying this framework to life sciences and software cases (e.g., Genetic Techs., Synopsys, TDE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-to inquiry (step 1): identification of patent-ineligible concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is evaluated to see if it is 'directed to' a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have characterized DNA correlations, thermodynamic relationships, and certain software algorithms as natural phenomena or abstract ideas. The analysis often shapes the remainder of the §101 inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement (step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional claim elements must provide an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely conventional or generic steps (e.g., storing, receiving, validating data; generic sensors or detectors) typically do not supply an inventive concept. Patentees can avoid invalidation by demonstrating an inventive leap beyond merely claiming a law of nature or abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: No claim dissection; evaluate the claimed invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility should be evaluated for the invention as a whole rather than by dissecting the claim into a judicially-excluded concept plus additional steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed legislation forbids dissecting claims into parts (a practice required by Mayo) and directs evaluation of the 'claimed invention' in its entirety. The text criticizes courts that divorce additional steps from the asserted natural phenomenon to reach ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude §§102/103/112 issues from §101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter eligibility analysis should not consider inventiveness/patentability issues that are addressed by other statutory sections (novelty, nonobviousness, enablement/definiteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal expressly prohibits consideration of 'inventiveness' and issues under §§102, 103, and 112 during the §101 inquiry, arguing that other parts of the statute are sufficient to address preemption and claim breadth concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-neutral, clearer statutory definition of eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter eligibility should be defined more clearly and in a technology-neutral manner in statute to reduce uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed text seeks to restore the scope of eligibility envisioned by Congress and to remove vague judicial exceptions that vary by technology; it also removes 'new' from §101 and ties eligibility to 'utility.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit judicial exceptions to those expressly defined by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the exceptions to eligibility that are set forth in statute (the Title) should apply; the statute should foreclose the development of future judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed §101(b) is intended to be the sole exception; the proposed text changes 'subject to the conditions and requirements' language to 'subject only to the exceptions and conditions set forth in this Title' to bar additional judicially-created exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility based on claimed invention (claimed-invention-centric analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility should be determined with reference to the 'claimed invention' (the claim as a whole), aligning §101 with §§102/103/112 which are claim-directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The draft statute emphasizes that eligibility is based on what is claimed (not a 'gist' or purpose), and that claim construction principles should apply to §101 as they do to other sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility tied to utility (not novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed amendment makes eligibility dependent on utility and removes 'new' from the §101 text to avoid conflating novelty with eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty and nonobviousness remain the proper domains of §§102 and 103; the statute should not use §101 to introduce separate novelty-like requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of the 'mental steps' / 'pencil and paper' test
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have treated analyzing information by steps people go through in their minds, or by mathematical algorithms, as abstract ideas; a human could perform similar steps with pencil and paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues this reasoning is flawed for computer and software inventions because a human with pencil and paper cannot replicate the physical/electronic effects produced by a computer. Anti-pattern: invalidating software claims solely because analogous mental steps exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical scope of the mental-steps doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally used to exclude methods that could only be performed in the human mind when no apparatus was disclosed; disclosure of apparatus for performing the process without human intervention historically made a process statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical distinction suggests courts should consider whether claims actually require human mental performance or instead disclose machinery/apparatus that performs the steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic physical elements insufficient to confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have characterized routine physical components (e.g., inertial sensors, radiation detectors, computers) as 'generic' and insufficient to impart eligibility under Alice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report criticizes treating common physical parts as mere 'generic' add-ons; if standard mechanical or electronic elements are deemed generic, that undermines claims that rely on new uses of known machines (contrary to §100(b)). Examples: Thales (inertial sensors), Exergen (radiation detector/thermometer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden/standard of proof in motions (contextual note)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases (e.g., Agilent), the court noted that a defendant must prove lack of inventive concept by clear and convincing evidence to succeed on certain motions (such as a motion to dismiss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a case-specific evidentiary point: at some procedural stages, invalidity must be shown by clear and convincing evidence; absence of inventive concept may not be established at pleadings stage without that showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using §101 to police patent quality or combat 'patent trolls'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 is not an appropriate mechanism for addressing low-quality patents or abusive enforcement; patent quality issues are better addressed by funding USPTO, examiner training, and other reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPO argues that using §101 as a sledgehammer to invalidate poor patents risks collateral damage to legitimate inventions; quality concerns relate to enablement, novelty, non-obviousness, and specificity, which are separate inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative remedies to restore intended scope of §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed legislation seeks to reverse certain Supreme Court rulings, restore a broader scope of subject-matter eligibility (e.g., 'anything under the sun made by man'), and simplify the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features include: (a) explicit entitlement to patent for 'whoever invents or discovers' and requiring patent issuance when statutory provisions are satisfied; (b) explicit bar on judicial exceptions beyond statute; (c) specific architecture for eligibility and exception text to make analysis technology-neutral.
